source.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis Needs a Group Action
source.authors: Louie Hong Yao; Yu-Hao Li; Sheng-Chao Liu

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives a theoretical refinement relevant to whether dictionary-learning features are canonical, but does not empirically test toy-model superposition or its sparsity-dependent geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no experiments on toy superposition or LLM feature geometry. The V5 row records its own mathematical argument about reconstruction-preserving latent transformations; cited empirical findings, including those about refusal directions and key-space eviction, are not recorded as results of this study.
record.test_reason: A theoretical position paper with no experiments. It discusses the superposition decomposition and dictionary learning inside a symmetry audit (Section 2, Section 5, Table 1). Its one point on dictionary learning is about loss symmetries, not about whether trained SAE features are complete, stable or canonical. Sparsity cutting the latent symmetry to signed permutations implies identifiability only up to sign and order, which does not by itself count against V5. The line 'reduced but generally not eliminated' is asserted without derivation or data. The paper therefore does not make a specific argument or report results on whether V5 holds, so it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors argue the Linear Representation Hypothesis is a family of claims, each set by a G-space (object plus equivalence group), an equivariant procedure and an invariant predicate. The group must include architecture-induced symmetries, which depend on where the representation is read. Studies should state these choices and check the symmetry of the whole multi-stage analysis.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical symmetry audit, not a toy-network implementation or sparsity/interference experiment of the kind used to study superposition.

fits_no_version.finding: Symmetry audit of dictionary learning. On the activation side, the reconstruction loss restricts admissible transformations to isometries. On the latent side, a coordinatewise sparsity penalty cuts the latent mixing symmetry W→WB to signed permutations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE/dictionary decompositions are defined only up to signed permutations of the latents and up to isometries of activation space. Geometric claims about SAE features (angles, norms) depend on the Euclidean geometry fixed by the loss.

record.problems: No empirical results test superposition or SAE feature stability; the relevant V5 conclusion is a general mathematical argument rather than an evaluation across trained models or runs.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were omitted. Statements about other studies are cited findings, not results of this paper.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweeps, interference or geometry results.
No test of capacity competition or feature importance.
No study of other causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement in LLMs and no SAE recovery.
No empirical or formal test of SAE feature completeness, stability across seeds, or canonicity. The only remark is on symmetries of the training loss.
Cites Engels et al. on circular day/month features and notes that multi-dimensional features live in Gr(k,V). There is no result of its own.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/tests classification and the V5 limits_scope label are dropped: no result or specific argument bears on V5 as stated. The paper's mentions of superposition (citing Toy Models) and of multidimensional features (citing Engels) are discussion only. Cited findings (Arditi, KeyDiff, Wollschläger, etc.) are correctly excluded as results.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network experiments, feature-count or sparsity sweeps, interference measurements, or geometric transition results.
No test of capacity pressure, polysemanticity, or how feature importance affects dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No investigation of alternative causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of feature distribution across LLM neurons or SAE recovery of sparse features.
No empirical assessment of SAE feature completeness or stability across models, runs, or settings.
The paper discusses multidimensional linear features generally, but does not establish that features in a superposition decomposition are multidimensional.

rows.subject: Dictionary learning (general)
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes reconstruction-preserving changes to latent coordinates and the symmetry restriction from coordinatewise sparsity.
rows.measure: Whether latent feature coordinates are uniquely identified by reconstruction and sparsity constraints
rows.value: Latent transformations W→WB and x→B−1x preserve reconstruction; a coordinatewise sparsity penalty reduces the mixing symmetry to signed permutations, and latent non-identifiability is generally not eliminated.
rows.note: This is a theoretical symmetry argument, not an empirical test of SAE feature stability or completeness.
rows.check: This row is a theoretical observation about the symmetries of the dictionary-learning loss, not a measured result on SAE features. The symmetry it describes (signed permutations) is ordinary relabelling ambiguity. It is not evidence that features are incomplete, unstable or non-canonical across runs. The 'partial' state is unsupported because no effect is measured. The value misattributes 'latent non-identifiability is generally not eliminated' to Section 5. Section 5 only states the reduction to signed permutations; the 'generally not eliminated' remark is an unproven aside in Section 2.

relation.reason: The paper discusses superposition decompositions and dictionary-learning symmetries without testing the listed superposition claims.

tranche.reason: The symmetry audit neither tests a catalog claim version nor uses superposition as a tool. Signed-permutation symmetry does not establish instability or incompleteness of learned SAE features.

source_check.notes: The row records a theoretical symmetry observation, not an empirical measurement. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased in the pack.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper argues that sparsity reduces, but does not generally eliminate, latent non-identifiability; this qualifies claims that the resulting features are canonical (r1).
